title: Sales negotiation playbook - SLA & tradeoffs
content:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic negotiation playbook for AEs and SEs dealing with procurement teams focused on SLAs, outage exposure, and unit economics for LLM endpoints. The goal: convert SLA and pricing pressure into controllable tradeoffs (capacity, routing, fallback, observability) rather than top-line discounts.

When to use this doc:
- Mid-to-late stage procurement where the buyer asks for commercial SLAs or discounts tied to availability, latency, or cost per token.
- Renewals where customers threaten to move to another LLM API on price.
- Enterprise deals with security/compliance requirements that drive need for Private/Dedicated.

One-line positioning to open the conversation:
"We optimize for predictable inference economics and availability by offering contractable capacity, automated fallback policies, and detailed token-level observability—so you're buying predictable outcomes, not just a lower per-token rate."

Quick cheat sheet (what buyers care most and our lever):
- Availability (uptime) -> Lever: Dedicated capacity + multi-region failover + SLA credits
- Tail latency (p95/p99) -> Lever: Reserved lanes, model routing, latency-prioritized pools
- Unit cost (per-token) -> Lever: batching, KV/prefix cache, quantized model variants, usage tiers
- Data isolation / compliance -> Lever: Private deployment / VPC, audit logs, KMS integration
- Quality/regressions -> Lever: pinned model versions + rollout canaries + eval baselines

Anchors & tradeable items for the AE to offer (ordered by impact):
1) Dedicated capacity (monthly commit) - highest predictability. Offer a capacity commitment instead of token discounts.
2) Model pinning + rollback windows - minimizes regression risk on model upgrades.
3) Enhanced observability - token-level billing breakdown, 90-day retention, and prioritized support.
4) Structured fallbacks - pre-approved model variants that trigger when primary capacity is exhausted.
5) Short-term price credit for adoption windows (one-off) - make this a finite ramp incentive.

Negotiation scripts & objection handling (short snippets):
Objection: "Your per-token price is higher than competitor X."
Response: "We price for predictable production economics. Competitor X's price may appear lower on paper but it often requires engineering work to achieve latency SLOs, and their fallback behavior can produce quality regressions. We can map your traffic profile and show an apples-to-apples cost with autoscaling/latency controls enabled."

Objection: "We need 99.95% SLA or we’ll take our workload elsewhere."
Response: "We can meet that for dedicated capacity with a multi-region plan and automated fallbacks. For hosted, we offer 99.9% with transparent incident credits. If you need 99.95% as a contractual requirement, the right path is Reserved/Dedicated + runbook alignment—here’s a sample commitment matrix and the delta in monthly pricing for that guarantee."

Objection: "We can’t expose tokens or logs."
Response: "We offer Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) with customer-managed KMS and configurable audit retention. For hosted customers we can provide sharded audit views and field-level masking—let’s map specific fields you cannot send and build a small onboarding checklist."

Objection: "If you go down, we lose revenue—give us a bigger credit."
Response: "Credits are one piece. We prioritize keeping your flows live via model fallbacks, multi-region routing, and warm reserved lanes. Credits are for remediation; our focus is preventing business-impacting outages. We’ll walk your ops team through the outage playbook during contract sign-off."

Competitive frame (how to contrast versus typical LLM API competitors):
- Competitor A: Low list price, limited tooling for latency/throughput controls -> Talk about our predictability levers and lower TCO for production workloads.
- Competitor B: Enterprise SLA but opaque performance (no token-level visibility) -> Highlight our billable telemetry and per-route dashboards.
- Competitor C: Strong open-source runtime but requires heavy ops -> Position Redwood as managed performance with the option to move private later.

Value metrics to use in deal math (examples to tailor to customer):
- tokens/day and 99th percentile latency target -> show required reserved qps and monthly dedicated GPU hours
- cost per 1M tokens (hosted) vs committed capacity unit (dedicated) -> show crossover point where dedicated becomes cheaper
- estimated engineering hours to self-host competitor -> convert to $ and compare to our managed premium

Pricing concession matrix (recommended negotiation play):
- Small discount (5–10%) tied to 12-month commit for Hosted with observability add-on.
- Larger delta (15–25%) available for Dedicated reserved capacity with >12-month commitment and usage minimums.
- Credits for uptime: cap credits to 2 months of fees; don’t accept uncapped liability.
- Free onboarding & eval window (30–90 days) with usage cap but no long-term discount commitments.

Ops-level technical traps to avoid (red flags for SE):
- Customer asks to include unlimited SLA credits or revenue guarantees. Escalate and push back—limit credits and pair with capacity commitments.
- Requests that require custom runtime changes. Use product/solutions to scope with costed statement of work.
- Demands for on-premification without security review. Use the compliance intake form and timeline (Private deployment 8–12 weeks typical).

Suggested play: "Safe Adoption Bundle" (sales motion for risk-averse buyers)
- 6–12 month adoption pact: Reduced per-token for first 6 months + Dedicated burst pool + 30-day rollback guarantee on model changes + two scheduled runbook dry-runs with SRE.
- Why it works: Lowers buyer’s perceived risk, creates observable metrics to convert to longer-term reserved contract.

Sample talktrack for AE during procurement meeting (5 minutes):
"We've mapped three levers that lock down cost and availability for production: contract capacity, observable usage, and automated fallbacks. For the initial phase we recommend a 6-month adoption bundle: we supply a reserved burst pool, double the retention on traces for 90 days so your SREs can validate, and a discounted ramp. If, after the trial, we see your 99th percentile latency and cost metrics meet targets, we can move to a committed Dedicated plan with a deeper discount and an SLA of 99.95%."

Appendix: Pre-call checklist for SE/AE
- Bring recent latency & cost benchmarks for a similar customer workload.
- Confirm whether customer needs Private or Dedicated. If Private, ensure compliance intake has been started.
- Prepare 2 fallback model variants with expected quality deltas.
- Have product runbooks and the standard SLA language ready to share.
- Know the cross-over math: at what tokens/day does Dedicated beat Hosted cost?

Open questions to surface to Product/Legal during negotiation:
- Maximum acceptable SLA credit percentage and cap for commercial renewals.
- Timeline and cost for expedited Private deployments (under 8 weeks).
- Any permanent product commitments we should avoid (experimental kernel changes, custom quantization requests).

Notes to self / follow ups:
- Build a templated "Adoption Bundle" term sheet for sales that includes runbook attachments, fallbacks, and onboarding milestones.
- Coordinate with Solutions Eng to create 3 example cross-over calculators for common workloads (chat, embeddings, reranking).
- Ask Legal to produce a short appendix listing typical credit calculations for outages (to avoid long email threads).

End of playbook.

[This doc is intentionally tactical — use it alongside the product SLA cheat sheet and the dedicated-capacity pricing sheet in Confluence. If this negotiation escalates, loop in PS and SRE for a joint technical procurement session.]
